item.research_question: What is the effect of cutting parameters (spindle speed and feed rate) and three types of cutting-tool coatings (TiN/TiAlN, TiAlN, and TiN) on the surface finish, form, and dimensional tolerances of holes drilled in Al6061-T651 alloy?
item.material_system: Al6061-T651 alloy (210 × 150 × 10 mm³, hardness 111.5–112.5 HV) drilled with 10 mm diameter carbide twist drills coated with TiN/TiAlN, TiAlN, or TiN.
item.processing_route: Dry drilling on a Rapimill 700-CNC milling machine using a full factorial design (3 levels of spindle speed: 1000, 2000, 3000 rpm; 3 levels of feed rate: 50, 100, 150 mm/min; 3 coatings), with each combination repeated three times for a total of 81 holes.
item.test_conditions: Dry cutting conditions; spindle speeds of 1000, 2000, and 3000 rpm; feed rates of 50, 100, and 150 mm/min; hole measurements taken at top (1 mm below upper surface) and bottom (1 mm above lower surface).
key_findings: All holes were oversized regardless of tool coating or cutting parameters, with hole size deviations ranging between 15.47 µm and 79.9 µm.
The highest surface roughness (Ra and Rz) occurred when using TiN-coated tools, particularly at n = 1000 rpm and f = 150 mm/min.
TiN-coated tools resulted in lower hole circularity at the entry and higher cylindricity compared to TiN/TiAlN and TiAlN coatings.
TiN/TiAlN and TiAlN coatings were more effective in reducing hole circularity when drilling at higher spindle speeds (n = 3000 rpm).
A white layer formed at the exit of holes drilled with TiN/TiAlN-coated tools, with an average thickness of 200 µm reaching up to 400 µm.
ANOVA analysis showed that tool coating contributed 23.9% to hole size deviation at the top and 16.8% at the bottom.
Intermediate spindle speeds (2000 rpm) and low feed rates (100–150 mm/min) generally provided the lowest surface roughness metrics across all coatings.
Material side flow was more likely to occur with TiN-coated tools due to their lower thermal stability and hardness compared to the other coatings.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the higher roughness and built-up edge on TiN tools to TiN's lower oxidation resistance, lower hardness, and higher chemical affinity with aluminum, which causes chips to diffuse and adhere to the tool surface. The formation of white layers on TiN/TiAlN and TiAlN tools is attributed to severe plastic deformation and high machining temperatures causing cut chips to melt and resolidify on the borehole surface, potentially involving chemical interaction with the coating materials.
item.limitations: The study notes that the repeatability of surface roughness was low, affecting ANOVA results. Additionally, the 3D surface analysis was limited to small areas and required many measurements along the hole depth, making it time-consuming. The study also did not consider factors such as fixture setup, dynamic interaction, vibrations, or tool deflections.
item.future_work: The authors state that the presence of aluminum in the TiN/TiAlN- and TiAlN-coated tools and its role in white layer formation will be the scope of a future study. They also propose that a new study will investigate factors such as fixture setup, dynamic interaction between the drill and workpiece, and resulting vibrations.
quotes: The highest surface roughness occurred when using TiN-coated tools.
All holes in this study were oversized regardless of the tool coating or cutting parameters used.

Optical microscopes revealed that a built-up edge and adhesions were most likely to form on TiN-coated tools due to TiN's chemical affinity and low oxidation temperature compared to the TiN/TiAlN and TiAlN coatings.

item.research_question: How do three types of cutting-tool coatings (TiN/TiAlN, TiAlN, and TiN) influence the hole surface roughness, dimensional tolerances, and edge quality when drilling Al6061-T651 alloy under varying cutting parameters?
item.material_system: Al6061-T651 aluminum alloy drilled with solid carbide twist drills coated with TiN, TiAlN, or TiN/TiAlN
item.processing_route: Dry drilling using solid carbide twist drills with fixed geometry; variables included spindle speed and feed rate
item.test_conditions: Dry drilling conditions; hole measurements taken at entry and exit; surface roughness (Ra, Rz), hole size, circularity, cylindricity, and perpendicularity evaluated
key_findings: Surface roughness Ra and Rz in most holes did not exceed 1 µm and 3 µm, respectively.
Holes drilled using TiN-coated tools had the highest surface roughness.
Holes produced were always oversized between 15 and 80 µm.
Hole circularity at the top and bottom ranged between 7 and 60 µm.
TiN/TiAlN-coated tools produced the worst hole cylindricity, especially at low and medium spindle speeds.
TiN-coated tools were more suitable for drilling at low cutting parameters, while TiN/TiAlN- and TiAlN-coated tools were better at higher parameters.
The contribution of the cutting-tool coating was more significant at the hole entry than at the exit.
Spindle speed had a major effect on hole perpendicularity compared to feed rate and tool coating.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the higher surface roughness of TiN tools to its lower oxidation temperature, lower hardness, and high affinity to react with aluminum. Built-up edge formation is linked to heat melting aluminum particles that weld to the tool, with TiN showing more accumulation due to lower thermal stability. TiN/TiAlN coatings produce superior exit edge quality with minimal burr, avoiding deburring needs.
item.limitations: A conclusion on the tool life for each of the coated tools could not be reached due to the limited number of holes drilled in this study.
item.future_work: The authors state the work aims to complement existing literature and fill the gap, as the effect of these three specific coatings on Al6061 was not previously investigated in a single study, implying a need for further comprehensive studies on tool life and broader parameter ranges.
quotes: The surface-roughness metrics Ra and Rz in most holes did not exceed 1 µm and 3 µm, respectively.
Holes drilled using TiN-coated tools had the highest surface roughness.
This would indicate that drilling using TiN/TiAlN-coated tools would produce holes with the minimal burr at the exit
